# Overview

This in-class exercise follows Lesson 8. It delineates the trade areas of 28 fast-food stores in Taichung City with the Huff model, using the **MCI** package. In class, the prof worked through a revised version of chapter 18 of the book.

# Getting Started

```{r}
#| output: false
pacman::p_load(sf, tidyverse, MCI, tmap, ggstatsplot)
```

# Importing Data

## Importing geospatial data

```{r}
#| output: false
stores <- st_read(
  dsn = "data/geospatial",
  layer = "STORES_TC")

town <- st_read(
  dsn = "data/geospatial",
  layer = "TOWN_TC")

village <- st_read(
  dsn = "data/geospatial",
  layer = "VILLAGE_TC")
```

## Importing aspatial data

```{r}
#| output: false
pop2019 <- read_csv(
  "data/aspatial/pop2019.csv")

store_sales <- read_csv(
  "data/aspatial/Store_sales_data.csv")
```

# Data Preparation

## Aggregating store sales

The code chunk below aggregates the store sales data by store code.

```{r}
store_sales_aggre <- store_sales %>%
  group_by(`Store Code`) %>%
  summarise(
    "Total_Bill" = sum(Bills, na.rm = TRUE),
    "Total_Sales" = sum(Amount, na.rm = TRUE))
```

## Relational join

In the code chunk below, `left_join()` of **dplyr** appends the sales totals to the stores, `mutate()` creates a new field called *Store_size*, and `st_drop_geometry()` drops the geometry.

```{r}
stores_tidied <- stores %>%
  left_join(store_sales_aggre,
            by = join_by(
              Store_CD == `Store Code`)) %>%
  mutate(Store_size = 1) %>%
  st_drop_geometry()
```

Next, `summary()` is used to check if there are any missing values in the data.frame.

```{r}
summary(stores_tidied)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning diary
This is where the prof changed the book. The result goes into a new object, `stores_tidied`, so `stores` keeps its geometry for mapping later. Every store now gets a size of 1 instead of 100. Since all stores share the same value, it cancels out of the Huff formula either way, so the probabilities do not change. `stores_tidied` has `r nrow(stores_tidied)` rows and `r ncol(stores_tidied)` columns, with no geometry.
:::

## Tidying pop2019 data.frame

Before appending pop2019 to the village sf data.frame, it is wise to check that the values in the join fields are the same.

```{r}
glimpse(pop2019)
```

```{r}
glimpse(village)
```

The village ID, *V_ID*, in pop2019 does not have the same structure as *VILLCODE* in the village sf data.frame. The code chunk below removes the "-" sign from the values.

```{r}
pop2019 <- pop2019 %>%
  mutate(V_ID = str_remove_all(
    V_ID, "-"))
```

Now, `left_join()` of **dplyr** appends the data in pop2019 onto the village sf data.frame.

```{r}
village <- village %>%
  left_join(pop2019,
            by = join_by(
              VILLCODE == V_ID))
```

## Check for missing or zero values

The code chunk below is used to check for any records with missing values.

```{r}
summary(village)
```

The output above reveals five missing values in the H_CNT, P_CNT, M_CNT and F_CNT fields. The code chunk below removes those five records from the village sf data.frame.

```{r}
village <- village %>%
  filter(!is.na(P_CNT))
```

```{r}
any(is.na(village$H_CNT))
any(is.na(village$P_CNT))
any(is.na(village$M_CNT))
any(is.na(village$F_CNT))
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning diary
After the join and the filter, `village` has `r nrow(village)` villages and `r ncol(village)` columns, the same as on the prof's screen. When he ran the join a second time in class, his `village` picked up columns like `COUNTY_ID.x` and `TOWN_ID.x`. The join chunk overwrites `village`, so running it again joins pop2019 a second time and dplyr adds `.x` and `.y` to keep the duplicate names apart. A clean render runs each chunk once, so it does not happen here.
:::

# Computing Distance Matrix

Instead of calculating the distance between the villages and the stores directly, the code chunk below takes a point inside each village with `st_point_on_surface()`, then computes the distance between those points and the stores.

```{r}
village_center <- st_point_on_surface(village)
distmat <- st_distance(village_center, stores)
```

Next, the code chunk below names the rows and columns with the village and store codes, and converts the distance matrix into a long data.frame format.

```{r}
rownames(distmat) <- village$`VILLCODE`
colnames(distmat) <- stores$`Store_CD`

distmat_long <- distmat %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column(var = "VILLCODE") %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -VILLCODE,
    names_to = "Store_CD",
    values_to = "distance"
  ) %>%
  mutate(distance = as.numeric(distance))
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning diary
`distmat` has one row for each of the `r nrow(distmat)` villages and one column for each of the `r ncol(distmat)` stores, so the long table has `r format(nrow(distmat_long), big.mark = ",")` rows, one per village and store pair. `st_distance()` returns the distances with units attached, so `as.numeric()` strips them to plain metres before the Huff model uses them.
:::

# Preparing Interaction Matrix

The code chunk below builds the interaction matrix required by the **MCI** package.

```{r}
ijMatrix <- distmat_long %>%
  left_join(
    stores_tidied %>%
      select(Store_CD, Store_size,
             Total_Sales),
    by = "Store_CD") %>%
  relocate(
    distance, .after = last_col())
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning diary
This step also differs from the book. The book calls the table `interaction_matrix` and has to drop the geometry from `stores` inside the join. Here it is `ijMatrix`, and because `stores_tidied` already has no geometry, it can be joined directly. The prof also carries `Total_Sales` into the table, next to `Store_size`, so each village and store pair now holds the store's actual sales as well. `ijMatrix` has `r format(nrow(ijMatrix), big.mark = ",")` rows and the columns `r paste(names(ijMatrix), collapse = ", ")`.
:::

The code chunk below tidies the village sf data frame. It keeps the village code, the number of households and the population, adds the average household size, *HH_SIZE*, and drops the geometry.

```{r}
village_tidied <- village %>%
  select(VILLCODE, H_CNT, P_CNT) %>%
  mutate(HH_SIZE = P_CNT/H_CNT) %>%
  st_drop_geometry()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning diary
*HH_SIZE* is the number of people per household. It ranges from `r round(min(village_tidied$HH_SIZE), 2)` to `r round(max(village_tidied$HH_SIZE), 2)` across the `r nrow(village_tidied)` villages, with a median of `r round(median(village_tidied$HH_SIZE), 2)`. This is new compared with the book, which only uses the total population, *P_CNT*.
:::

The code chunk below appends the fields from the village_tidied data frame to ijMatrix.

```{r}
ijMatrix <- ijMatrix %>%
  left_join(
    village_tidied,
    by = "VILLCODE") %>%
  relocate(
    HH_SIZE, .after = last_col())
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning diary
Each row of `ijMatrix` is now one village and store pair with everything the model needs, the store's size and sales, the distance, and the village's households, population and household size. It has `r format(nrow(ijMatrix), big.mark = ",")` rows and `r ncol(ijMatrix)` columns. *HH_SIZE* is already the last column after the join, so `relocate()` does not move anything here. Like the village join earlier, this chunk overwrites `ijMatrix`, so running it twice in a live session would add `.x` and `.y` columns.
:::

# Computing Huff Model

`huff.shares()` of **MCI** computes the probability that the people in each village choose each store.

```{r}
huff_share <- huff.shares(
  ijMatrix, "VILLCODE", "Store_CD",
  "Store_size", "distance", lambda = -1.28)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning diary
The prof sets `lambda = -1.28` instead of the default of -2 used in the book. In the lesson's formula this is the distance exponent λ, so a smaller value means distance puts people off less, and a store draws customers from further away. In my Hands-on Exercise 8, fitting λ to the stores' actual sales shares also gave a value well below 2, at λ = 1, so both point the same way.
:::

## Trade area analysis for a single store

First, the code chunk below selects the market share data of one store by its *Store_CD*, store BT.

```{r}
market_share <- huff_share %>%
  filter(Store_CD == "BT")
```

Next, the trade areas of the selected store are derived by joining its market share to the villages.

```{r}
Trade_area <- village %>%
  left_join(market_share)
```

Before plotting the trade area map, the code chunk below extracts the selected store from the stores sf data.frame.

```{r}
selected_store <- stores %>%
  filter(Store_CD == "BT")
```

The prof plots the map with the same code as the book. I reuse my map from Hands-on Exercise 8, which labels the classes with two significant figures, greys out the five villages without residents, and shows the other 27 stores as white dots.

::: panel-tabset
## The Plot

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
fmt_num <- function(v) {
  sapply(v, function(z) {
    if (abs(z) < 0.01) formatC(z, format = "e", digits = 1)
    else formatC(signif(z, 2), format = "fg", digits = 2)
  }) %>% trimws()
}

q <- quantile(Trade_area$p_ij, probs = seq(0, 1, length.out = 11))

tm_shape(town) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "grey80", col = NA) +
tm_shape(Trade_area) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "p_ij",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(q[1:10], Inf) %>% unname(),
                labels = paste(fmt_num(q[1:10]), "to", fmt_num(q[2:11])),
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Patronage Probability",
                                      position = tm_pos_out("right", "center")),
              col = "grey80", lwd = 0.3) +
tm_shape(stores) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.45, fill = "white", col = "black", lwd = 1.2) +
tm_shape(selected_store) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.6, fill = "#D55E00", col = "black") +
  tm_title("Distribution of Patronage Probability of Store BT by village",
           size = 1.3, fontface = "bold") +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2, position = c("right", "top")) +
  tm_scalebar(position = c("left", "bottom"))
```

}

:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning diary
With λ = 1.28, BT's lowest probability in any village is `r signif(min(Trade_area$p_ij), 2)`, against about 0.0001 with the book's λ = 2 in my Hands-on Exercise 8. A gentler distance decay spreads each village's choice more evenly across the stores, so far villages give BT a larger share than before. BT still has a probability above one half in `r sum(Trade_area$p_ij > 0.5)` villages.
:::

The code chunk below turns the probabilities into a wide table, one row per village and one column per store.

```{r}
huff_share_wider <- huff_share %>%
  select(VILLCODE, Store_CD, p_ij) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Store_CD,
              values_from = p_ij)
```

## Trade areas of all stores

Each village is given to the store it has the highest probability of patronising. In the code chunk below, `pick(2:29)` takes the 28 store columns of `huff_share_wider`, `max.col()` finds the column with the highest probability in each row, and `names()` turns it into the store code, saved as a new field, *TA*. `ties.method = "first"` means that if two stores tie for the highest probability, the first one is used.

```{r}
huff_TA <- huff_share_wider %>%
  mutate(
    TA = names(pick(2:29))[
      max.col(pick(2:29),
              ties.method = "first")
    ]
  )
```

The code chunk below keeps only the village code and its trade area, then appends the trade area of each village to the village sf data.frame.

```{r}
huff_TA_tidied <- huff_TA %>%
  select(VILLCODE, TA)

village_TA <- village %>%
  left_join(huff_TA_tidied,
            by = join_by(VILLCODE))
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning diary
The prof pointed out that some of these steps are redundant and can be nested. `huff_TA` and `huff_TA_tidied` are only stepping stones, so the two chunks above can be written as one pipe. I check that it gives the same trade areas.

```{r}
village_TA_nested <- huff_share_wider %>%
  mutate(TA = names(pick(2:29))[
    max.col(pick(2:29), ties.method = "first")]) %>%
  select(VILLCODE, TA) %>%
  left_join(village, ., by = join_by(VILLCODE))

identical(village_TA$TA, village_TA_nested$TA)
```

The same applies earlier. `village_tidied` is only used to join household size onto `ijMatrix`, so it could be piped straight into that join. Keeping the steps separate makes each object easy to `View()` in class, while nesting keeps the environment tidy.
:::

`summarise()` merges the villages of each store into one trade area, so the map can draw the boundaries between them.

```{r}
TA_areas <- village_TA %>%
  group_by(TA) %>%
  summarise()
```

::: panel-tabset

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning diary
The prof maps the trade areas with `tm_polygons(fill = "TA")`. tmap's default palette only has a handful of colours, so with 28 stores it repeats them, and several stores share the same colour on his map. I build 28 different colours with `hcl()`, using only reds, oranges, browns, blues and purples and leaving out the green hues, and I alternate dark and light so stores next to each other in the legend stand apart. I also draw the boundary of each trade area and label each store with its code, so the map can be read without matching colours to the legend.

Because every store has the same size, the store with the highest probability is always the nearest one, whatever λ is. A smaller λ makes the probabilities more even, but it never changes which store comes first. I check this against the nearest store of each village.

```{r}
nearest <- distmat_long %>%
  group_by(VILLCODE) %>%
  slice_min(distance, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup()
nearest_store <- setNames(nearest$Store_CD, nearest$VILLCODE)
```

`r round(mean(village_TA$TA == nearest_store[village_TA$VILLCODE]) * 100)` percent of villages go to their nearest store. The trade areas would only differ from nearest-store areas if the stores had different sizes.
:::
